title: DSA timed mock and pattern map
goal: Solve interview-style problems under time pressure and build a one-page map of every pattern you know.

concepts: Recognising the pattern from the problem's wording
Big-O for time and space; explaining it in one sentence
Brute force first, then optimise, saying both aloud
Edge cases: empty input, one element, duplicates, negatives, huge input
Recovering when stuck: smaller example, draw it, relax a constraint

resources.title: NeetCode roadmap (free problem lists by pattern)
Tech Interview Handbook: Algorithms study cheatsheet

build.task: Do a 90-minute timed mock: 3 unseen problems (one easy, two medium; pick from LeetCode's Top Interview 150 list problems you haven't solved), 30 minutes each, speaking your approach aloud (record audio). For each: write the brute-force approach and its complexity before coding, then the optimised one. Afterwards write interview/pattern-map.md: one row per pattern you learned (hashing, two pointers, sliding window, stack, binary search, linked list, trees, BST, graphs, heaps, DP, backtracking) with 'signals in the problem statement', the template idea, complexity, and 2 problems you solved.
acceptance: 3 timed problems attempted with audio recorded
Brute force and optimised approaches written with complexity for each
At least 2 of 3 accepted within time (or a written analysis of what blocked you)
pattern-map.md covers all 12 patterns with signals, template, complexity and examples

hints: Signals: 'sorted array' → binary search or two pointers; 'contiguous subarray/substring' → sliding window; 'next greater' → monotonic stack; 'top k' → heap; 'number of ways / min cost' → DP; 'all combinations' → backtracking; 'shortest path in a grid' → BFS.
If you're stuck for 5 minutes, say the brute force aloud and code it. A working O(n²) beats an unfinished O(n).
Always state complexity at the end without being asked: 'This is O(n) time and O(n) space because of the map.'
proof: Commit with pattern-map.md and your three solutions.

explainBack.q: How do you decide which pattern a new problem needs?
lookFor: look for signals in the wording
start from brute force and find the waste

explainBack.q: Explain the time and space complexity of one of today's solutions.

lastHintExplanation: Interview problems are mostly familiar patterns in disguise. The wording ('sorted', 'contiguous', 'top k', 'number of ways') and the input size (n up to 10⁵ means O(n log n) or better) point to the right tool. Stating the brute force first shows clear thinking and gives you a fallback if the optimisation doesn't come.

title: System design basics: a URL shortener
goal: Learn a simple framework for system design questions and apply it to a classic example.

concepts: Framework: requirements (functional and non-functional), estimates, API, data model, high-level design, deep dive, trade-offs
Back-of-the-envelope estimates: requests per second, storage per year
Generating short codes: random base62 vs counter + base62, and collisions
Read-heavy systems: caching (Redis), CDNs, database indexes
Scaling basics: stateless servers behind a load balancer, read replicas
301 vs 302 redirects; rate limiting abuse; analytics

build.task: In jobready-journey, write interview/system-design-url-shortener.md following the framework: requirements; estimates (assume 1 million new links a month and 100 reads per link); the API (POST /links, GET /:code); the data model; a diagram (Mermaid) with load balancer, app servers, cache and database; the code-generation choice with collision handling; caching strategy; and 5 trade-offs. Then build a tiny version in Express + PostgreSQL (or extend api-starter): POST /links creates a code, GET /:code redirects with 302 and increments a click count, with tests. Write a short section applying the same framework to 'design ApplyTrack for 1 million users'.
acceptance: Design doc follows the framework from requirements to trade-offs
Estimates shown with working (requests per second, storage)
Mermaid diagram renders
Working mini shortener with tests (create, redirect, 404, click count)
A section scaling ApplyTrack to 1 million users

hints: Estimates: 1M links a month ≈ 0.4 writes per second; 100M reads a month ≈ 40 reads per second on average (peaks maybe 10× that). Storage: 1M × 500 bytes ≈ 500 MB a month.
Base62 (0–9, a–z, A–Z) with 7 characters gives 62⁷ ≈ 3.5 trillion codes. With random codes, rely on a UNIQUE constraint and retry on collision.
302 (temporary) lets you count every click because browsers don't cache it; 301 is cached by browsers, which is faster but hides repeat clicks.
proof: Commit with the design doc and the mini shortener.

explainBack.q: Walk through your URL shortener design in 5 minutes.
Why use 302 instead of 301 for the redirect?

lastHintExplanation: Junior system design rounds test structured thinking, not perfect answers. Clarify requirements, estimate scale, define the API and data, draw the main components, then discuss trade-offs. A URL shortener is read-heavy, so a cache in front of the database does most of the work, and 302 redirects keep analytics accurate at the cost of more traffic.

title: HR and behavioural round
goal: Handle the HR round confidently: motivation, salary, relocation, gaps and offers.

concepts: Common HR questions: why this company, strengths and weaknesses, five-year goals, why should we hire you
Explaining a non-traditional path or a gap positively and honestly
Salary expectations: research ranges first, give a range, consider the total package
Questions about relocation, shifts, bonds and notice periods
Reading an offer letter: CTC vs in-hand pay, bond clauses, probation, joining date
Professional follow-up emails and handling rejection

build.task: In jobready-journey, write interview/hr.md with honest answers for 15 HR questions (including 'why should we hire you?', 'what's your weakness?', 'where do you see yourself in 5 years?', 'why did you choose this field?', 'what are your salary expectations?', 'are you OK with relocation or night shifts?' and 'do you have other offers?'). Research the salary range for junior frontend/full-stack roles in your city on 2–3 sites and write your range with the reasoning. Write templates for a thank-you email after an interview, a polite follow-up after a week of silence, and a reply to a rejection that asks for feedback. List 5 red flags to check in any offer letter.
acceptance: 15 HR answers, honest and specific to you
A researched salary range with sources
3 email templates written
5 offer-letter red flags listed (e.g. long bonds, unclear CTC split)
Answers practised aloud at least once

hints: Weakness answers work best when they're real and show progress: 'I used to spend too long polishing before asking for feedback; now I share early drafts, as I did with my capstone pull requests.'

Salary: 'Based on my research for junior full-stack roles in this city, I'm looking for ₹X–Y LPA, but I'm flexible for the right learning opportunity.' Know the difference between CTC and in-hand pay.
A service bond (for example 2 years with a large penalty) is a serious commitment. Read it fully, ask questions, and decide deliberately.
proof: Commit with interview/hr.md (keep any personal salary details private if you prefer).

explainBack.q: Answer 'Why should we hire you?' now.
What's the difference between CTC and in-hand salary?
lookFor: CTC includes employer PF, gratuity, bonuses, benefits
in-hand is monthly take-home after deductions
compare offers on in-hand and growth

lastHintExplanation: HR rounds check motivation, honesty and fit. Specific answers backed by evidence (your deployed projects, your 26-week routine) beat generic ones. CTC (cost to company) includes items such as the employer's PF contribution, gratuity, variable pay and benefits, so in-hand monthly pay can be noticeably lower. Always compare offers on in-hand pay, terms such as bonds, and learning potential.

title: Job search strategy and tailored applications
goal: Build a steady, trackable job search system and send your first batch of strong applications.

concepts: Channels: job boards, company career pages, referrals, LinkedIn outreach, off-campus drives, communities
Referrals and warm outreach beat cold applications
Tailoring: resume keywords, a 3-line cover note, the most relevant project first
Tracking every application (dogfood ApplyTrack!)
A weekly routine: applications, outreach, practice, learning
Avoiding scams: never pay for a job, check the company domain

resources.title: Government of India: National Career Service

build.task: Write interview/job-search-plan.md: target roles (e.g. Junior Frontend Developer, Angular Developer, Full-Stack Developer Trainee), 3 cities or remote, 25 target companies (startups, product firms and service companies), the channels you'll use, and a weekly routine (e.g. 10 tailored applications, 5 outreach messages, 3 DSA problems, 1 mock). Write a LinkedIn outreach template for asking for a referral (short, specific, polite). Then send your first 5 tailored applications today, tracking each in your own ApplyTrack with the job URL, source and notes.
acceptance: job-search-plan.md with roles, locations, 25 companies, channels and a weekly routine
A referral outreach template
5 real, tailored applications sent today
All 5 tracked in ApplyTrack
A note on how you'll spot and avoid job scams

hints: Outreach template: 'Hi <name>, I'm a full-stack developer (Angular, Node, PostgreSQL) and I saw the <role> opening at <company>. I built <project + link>, which uses <relevant tech>. Would you be open to referring me, or sharing what the team looks for? Thank you!'
Tailor the top third of your resume (summary, skills order, first project) for each role. Keep a master resume and save each tailored copy with the company name.
Red flags: fees for training or 'registration', personal email domains for HR, offers without any interview, pressure to decide immediately.
proof: Commit with job-search-plan.md, and a screenshot of your ApplyTrack board with the 5 applications.

explainBack.q: Why are referrals so much more effective than cold applications?
lookFor: resume gets seen by a human

explainBack.q: What's your weekly job search routine, and how will you measure it?

lastHintExplanation: Big job posts receive hundreds of applications, and a referral puts yours in front of a person. A steady weekly routine with numbers you can track (applications, outreach, response rate in your own ApplyTrack dashboard) turns job hunting from luck into a process you can improve.

title: Mock interview 2: full loop
goal: Run a complete interview loop (technical, project and HR) and measure your improvement since mock 1.

concepts: A full loop: online test → technical round → project/managerial round → HR
Consistency across rounds
Comparing against mock 1: what improved, what didn't
Keeping energy and focus across a long day

build.task: Do a 2-hour mock loop, ideally with a different person from mock 1: (1) a 20-minute online-style test (10 aptitude questions + 2 output-prediction JS questions); (2) a 45-minute technical round (concepts + one live coding problem + one small UI task such as 'build a star rating component'); (3) a 30-minute project round on StandupBoard (security model, real-time design, what you'd change); (4) a 15-minute HR round. Record what you can. Write interview/mock2-review.md: the same scores as mock 1 side by side, 3 improvements, 3 remaining gaps and a plan for each.
acceptance: All 4 parts of the loop completed
Scores compared with mock 1
3 improvements and 3 gaps with specific plans
Feedback from the mock interviewer recorded (if a person did it)

hints: Use your own content for the online test: pick aptitude questions from earlier days that you got wrong.
For the StandupBoard round, practise drawing the security layers: Firebase Auth → security rules for direct client access → verified ID tokens and checks in the Express API.
Treat it like the real thing: dress as you would, sit at a desk, and close other tabs.

explainBack.q: Explain StandupBoard's security model in 2 minutes.
lookFor: rules enforce membership/ownership/validation for client writes
Express verifies ID tokens and checks roles
Admin SDK bypasses rules so API must check

explainBack.q: What improved most since mock 1, and what's still your biggest gap?

lastHintExplanation: Real hiring loops test the same person from several angles, so consistency matters: the project you describe in HR should match what you explain technically. Comparing mock scores turns practice into measurable progress and tells you exactly where your final effort should go.
